title: Circular Motion and Races
tagline: Year 3 — Races, start and beat, dead heats and time lead on straight and circular courses

introduction.overview: A race compares the distance covered by competitors in the same time, or the time they take for the same distance. Terms such as "beats by", "gives a start of" and "dead heat" have precise meanings. On a circular course the same ideas combine with laps. The central fact is that in the same time the distances are in the ratio of the speeds.
introduction.placementRelevance: Race questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, usually with three runners and the phrase "A beats B by x metres and B beats C by y metres".
introduction.realWorldContext: Athletics events, handicap races and relay timings use these calculations.

learningObjectives: Compare three runners by chaining ratios
Convert distance leads to time leads and back
Handle races where a runner is given a start
Apply lap ideas to races on circular courses

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: In equal times, distance ∝ speed. In covering equal distance, time ∝ 1/speed.

coreDefinitions: A beats B by d metres: when A finishes, B is d metres behind.
A beats B by t seconds: B reaches the finish t seconds after A.
A gives B a start of d metres: B begins d metres ahead of A.
Dead heat: both reach the finish at the same time.
Winning margin in time = (distance lead) ÷ (loser's speed).
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A race result is a snapshot at the moment the winner finishes. At that instant the winner has covered the whole distance and the loser has covered the distance minus the margin, so the ratio of speeds is (race distance) : (race distance − margin).
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Write the speed ratio from "when A finishes, B has covered …". For three runners, chain the ratios by making the middle runner equal in both.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Speed ratio from a beat
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: D is the race distance, d the margin.
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: A beats B by 100 m in 1000 m → 10 : 9

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Chained races
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: If A : B = p : q and B : C = r : s then A : C = pr : qs
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Beats by 10 and 10 in 100 m → A beats C by 19

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Time margin
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Time lead = distance lead ÷ loser's speed

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Start given
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: B starts d metres ahead; A must cover D, B covers D − d

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Races on a circle
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Laps: speed ratio = ratio of laps in the same time

mainNarrative: A beats B by 100 m in a 1,000 m race means that when A has run 1,000 m, B has run 900 m. The speeds are in the ratio 1000 : 900 = 10 : 9. If A runs at 10 m/s, B runs at 9 m/s.

To compare three runners, chain the ratios through the middle one. If A beats B by 10 m in 100 m and B beats C by 10 m in 100 m, then A : B = 100 : 90 and B : C = 100 : 90. So A : C = 100 × 100 : 90 × 90 = 10000 : 8100, and when A runs 100 m, C runs 81 m: A beats C by 19 m.
Time leads: if A beats B by 20 m and B runs at 4 m/s, then B needs another 20 ÷ 4 = 5 s to reach the finish, so A beats B by 5 seconds.
Giving a start: if A gives B a start of 20 m in a 200 m race, A runs 200 m while B runs 180 m. They reach together (dead heat) if the speed ratio is 200 : 180 = 10 : 9.

On a circular course, the faster runner "beating" the slower by one lap means he covers one lap more in the same time. If A runs at 8 m/s and B at 6 m/s on a 400 m track, A laps B after 400 ÷ 2 = 200 s.

deepDiveAspects.title: Who wins depends on the distance
deepDiveAspects.content: A start that gives a dead heat in 200 m gives A a win in a longer race, because the faster runner gains more the farther they run.

deepDiveAspects.title: Combining margins
deepDiveAspects.content: Margins do not add. Chain the speed ratios; 10 m + 10 m in a 100 m race does not make 20 m.

solvedExamples.title: Chained races
solvedExamples.question: In a 100 m race A beats B by 10 m and B beats C by 10 m. By how many metres does A beat C?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: C runs 81% of what A runs.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Adding the margins to get 20 m.

solvedExamples.title: Time lead
solvedExamples.question: In a 200 m race A beats B by 20 m. B runs at 4 m/s. By how many seconds does A win?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: B still has to run 20 m.

solvedExamples.title: Start and dead heat
solvedExamples.question: A can run 200 m while B runs 180 m. In a 200 m race, what start must A give B for a dead heat?

steps.title: B runs
steps.explanation: When A runs 200 m, B runs 180 m.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: B has to cover 20 m less.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Giving B a start of 10 m.

shortcutMethods.title: Ratio from the snapshot

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Write the speed ratio as D : (D − margin) and chain ratios through the middle runner.

rulesForApplication: Speed ratio = distances in equal time.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Wrong speed for the time lead.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: A beats C by more than A beats B when B beats C by a positive margin.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Always state "when A finishes, B has run …".

selfCheckQuestions: Can I find the time lead?
Can I find the start for a dead heat?
